It is all about timing, we need the right leadership at the right time - and now we're in the position to determine the next step. - John
Other industries are being heavily disrupted by technology, and if we're not on a disruptive journey every day - we're going to be affected later on. - Theo
We are a strong co-op, and now we're starting to grow our sustainability and innovation. We need someone dedicated to that in the next 5-7 years. - Theo
In China, we opted for a partnership in an area where we needed more access at the time - infant nutrition. - Theo
Our investment in China continues to be long term - it doesn't come without risk and we continue to balance out that risk. - John
We have an integrated strategy in China, and overall it is going very very well. Yes, there are roadblocks, and we don't have easy access into markets like China - John
We started the succession plan in November and the announcement has moved forward instead of intended in April. - John
Extraordinary contribution and we'll know Theo will work to the very last second. - John
Fonterra remains extremely close to my heart, - Theo
I'm approaching 7 years, and it's been quite a ride but when I came in, I said I see Fonterra as the envy of the dairy world, and that is still the case - Theo

We are in the process of the CEO succession plan, and we're committed to the smooth transition to the next Chief Executive. We do envisage that even with the new CEO, Theo remains in an advisory role. - John
We remain positive on the outlook for the full year, and this is reflected in our forecast payout of $6.80-6.90. - John
We continue to have significant investments in our cream cheese plant and other key plants. - John
In summary, we've seen good ingredients results, but our consumer and foodservice is experiencing tighter margins - John
Our Gearing ratio remains strong, working capital is up 12 days. Strong picture overall on the balance sheet. - Marc
Foodservice: product mix shift, including a shift from butter to cream. We've lifted sales by 7% but still impacted by increase commodity prices. - Marc
Lower sales volumes this half due to record low opening inventories and low NZ milk collections for the season to date. However from the volume, we've put them into value products. - Marc
In Australia: The turnaround in our Australia business continues to gather momentum - Theo
Our China Farms are a CAPEX investment, but currently does not reflect the downstream value we'll get from Hema/Alibaba and Starbucks. - Theo
Early days but the supply of our fresh milk to Hema stores (part of Alibaba) is example of how we are moving our milk up the value chain. And Starbucks as well. - Theo
The market in China is changing – shifted from ambient to fresh milk. China's market for fresh food is growing particularly with dairy. - Theo

We do not have direct control over the company but we are influencing its direction and continue to call for an urgent business transformation by working co-operatively with Beingmate’s founder and majority shareholder - Theo
The strategic rationale holds for our partnership with Beingmate. The infant formula market in China is very attractive. Beingmate has the brands to participate strongly in this market - Theo

Our business in China has grown significantly in both volume and earnings. China contributes nearly a quarter of the Co-operative’s gross margin, even more potential with improved performance from our China farms - Theo
77% of the milk going into China comes from NZ, so it is important market and will continue to be strategically for us. - Theo
There will be a lot more information on China coming out soon, as this is part of our integrated strategy. It remains important in our Ingredients and Foodservice - Theo
Foodservice, we are not selling less than last year and given the current prices, this result is good. And we continue to shift milk to higher value. - Theo

Normalisations are when abnormal items are added back or deducted from Reported NPAT to give a better refection of the normal operations of the business and enable better comparisons between the periods - Marc

A strong Ingredients performance, generating normalised EBIT of $558 million, up nine per cent - Theo

Q1 was a very tough quarter, Q2 was very strong, and we expect the same for the remaining quarters. Normalised EBIT down by 25% mainly due to lower EBIT contribution from Consumer and Foodservice – down $120m. - Theo
Fonterra Forecast cash pay-out is globally competitive. Ahead of both EU and US. Important that we maintain a competitive milk price for the long term success of Fonterra - Theo
In Europe: we watching spring production as may have an impact on prices. In particular EU milk supply and inventory weighing on sentiment for global SMP - Theo #FonterraResults
Latin America continues to absorb supply, Russia we continue to see the results of the existing embargo. - Theo #FonterraResults

This New Zealand Sign Language Week, we’re proud to share the story of Joe, a Tanker Operator at our Clandeboye site in South Canterbury.

Joe’s day looks much like anyone else’s on site, but behind the scenes, small, thoughtful changes have helped create an inclusive, deaf‑aware environment where everyone feels supported and respected.

From live transcription during training to simple adjustments in how the team communicates day to day, Joe says it’s made a huge difference.

“I feel like I’m treated as an equal here. I’m the same as every other member of the team.”

New Zealand Sign Language is one of Aotearoa’s three official languages, and this week is about building understanding, connection and inclusion. 💙

It’s been one year since the launch of our Climate Roadmap, and we’re making progress towards our climate goals, including being coal free in our North Island manufacturing.  

We turned off the coal boiler at our Waitoa site this month, our last in the North Island marking a significant milestone in achieving our emissions reduction targets.
 
Here’s some key takeaway points on our progress so far:
 
🌱 Our near-term climate targets have been validated by the Science Based Targets Initiative (SBTi). This means SBTi have classified Fonterra's targets as in line with a 1.5°C future.
🌱 We’ve reduced Scope 1 and Scope 2 GHG emissions by 18.5% between FY18 and FY24.
🌱 We launched the NZMP Carbon Footprinter. This tool enables customers to understand the average emissions footprint of our key New Zealand-sourced NZMP products. Check it out here: https://www.nzmp.com/global/en/sustainability/carbon-footprinter.html 
🌱 We’ve continued to fund AgriZeroNZ, a joint venture, who have committed over $34 million in several methane mitigation technologies and R&D.
🌱 By the end of 2024 we will have achieved a 40% reduction in the number of New Zealand sites using coal from a FY18 base year.
 
Whilst we’re on track with our action plan to deliver our 2030 climate targets, there’s still more work to do.
 
Visit our website to learn more about our Climate Roadmap and next steps: https://www.fonterra.com/nz/en/sustainability/responsible-business/reporting.html#climate-roadmap

Last week, our Digital team joined Mauku School and Trees for Survival to plant almost 900 trees alongside a waterway on a farm in South Auckland 🌱

Planting native trees along waterways prevents erosion, slows flooding and improves the water quality of streams and wetlands, while providing habitat for our taonga birds and insects.

Some of the trees planted included hebe, toetoe, karamū, kānuka, tī kōuka (cabbage tree) and harakeke (flax).
 
“An absolutely fantastic day planting with Mauku School and their team of supporters. The hope is that they will take away small pieces of knowledge and inspiration for the environment, all the while restoring the biodiversity to land and improving the waterways.” – Paula Marx, South Auckland Facilitator at Trees for Survival. 
 
Trees for Survival is a charitable trust which works with over 200 schools and local communities across NZ to grow and plant native trees along waterways and on erosion prone hillsides. They’re an environmental education programme teaching the importance of native plants on native ecology.
 
Donate a plant today through Trees for Survival here: https://www.tfsnz.org.nz/shop/

South Waikato farming power couple Jess and Ev Mardell have harmonized water quality, biodiversity, and aesthetic values without disrupting their daily farming activities. The journey started during a Farm Environmental Plan (FEP) assessment, where they discovered a boggy area near their drainage system.

Guided by their Fonterra  Sustainable Dairy Adviser and NZ Landcare Trust’s Nathan Burkepile, the Mardells transformed this challenge into an opportunity. What's truly special is that they achieved this without any external funding, showcasing the potential within active farming systems🌱

Fonterra's 1600 tanker drivers transfer milk across the country. Their heavy load and 90km/h speed limit often means they travel slower than most people. Be patient around heavy vehicles such as tankers and large trucks—only pass when it's safe.
 
Because it takes longer to pass a heavy vehicle than it does to pass a car, make sure you have plenty of clear road ahead to safely pass without going over the speed limit.

If you're passing, you need to leave a large gap to a heavy vehicle before you move in front of them—because of its weight and the design of its brakes, at 90km/h it takes a heavy vehicle more than twice as far to stop as it takes a car.

Getting active in nature is a proven method of improving mental health. That’s how Surfing for Farmers (SFF) was started – to give farmers an outlet away from the pressures of work.

Over the past five years, SFF has experienced remarkable growth, expanding to 27 locations nationwide. Mānawatia a Matariki — Happy Māori New Year!

We've celebrated the week of Matariki by speaking with some of our people to learn what it means to them.

For Mohi Beckham, Matariki signals the beginnings of the Māori new year which provides environmental, social, spiritual and cultural annual guidelines. It is the beginning of Maramataka, the Māori lunar-stella calendar which has become an important part of his life on the farm.

“Since we took on the farm, we’ve been focused on regen farming, using more sustainable practices to improve the overall health of the farm. We started aligning our farming methods to the maramataka around eight months ago and although its early days we’ve seen some really positive changes.”

Read more on Mohi's story here: https://www.fonterra.com/nz/en/our-stories/articles/embracing-traditional-maori-farming.html

Can seaweed reduce greenhouse gas emissions? 

Over the past two years Fonterra in partnership with @seaforestaustralia have been exploring whether the use of Asparagopsis seaweed as a natural supplement feed for dairy cows could reduce greenhouse gas emissions. We are now ready to expand the trial to the next phase testing the supplement’s application at a commercially relevant scale. 

This is one of a number of solutions we are looking at to help solve the methane challenge.

Here is the first in a series of stories from our people:

Our Whānau - Te Reo Te Rangi ‘T’ - Tanker Driver, Waikato

"Pretty much my whole life’s been spent on the road. I’m always coming, going, or on the way. So it’s no surprise that I’ve had a long career in the transport industry. Yip, that sounds about right to me. 

When I was growing up, life was tough. I probably experienced things some kids would not want to experience growing up. I decided I wanted to break that cycle, so at 17 I joined the NZ Army. I didn’t expect it, but it had kids from the same situation as myself, and so they became my family for more than 12 years whilst I was there. They are still my “Brothers and Sisters” from another Mother.

When I left, I knew that working in transport was another make or break moment to do something good with my life. But those long shifts on the road aren’t easy on you or the family and my early jobs took a pretty big toll, especially on the kids. I wish that could have been a bit different.

Driving for a living, there’s a lot of time to reflect. It made me want to tap into my roots and give back, and for me those roots were the Army. I’ve been a volunteer with the Order of St John for 17 years, including the last 7 years, with the New Zealand Cadet Forces. As a New Zealand Cadet Force Officer, we see kids come and go that remind me of myself. The Cadets are full of kids just like I was. We teach them how to be safe, how to be New Zealand’s next leaders. It’s life changing for them, just like it was for me.

These days, you won’t actually find me too far from home. Driving for Fonterra means I don’t have to travel those long distances. I can finally sit still and watch my kids grow up. I sometimes go down to their school and have lunch with them - we all think that’s pretty cool. Some of the other kids get envious. My kids come with me to the St John’s events and volunteer their time too, showing big and little kids alike around the ambulance. It’s nice to be able to share those lessons, make other people feel good, show respect for the jobs and roles we play in the community. And yeah, it’s nice to finally stop moving too."

We’re doing everything we can to keep our people and communities safe. To help out with the current hand sanitiser shortage we’re making available 250,000 litres of high-grade ethanol to New Zealand companies, and working with the Government to prioritise where that should go. We’re increasing capacity with a target of producing an extra 220,000 litres of ethanol. We’re also working with Gull to test 250,000 litres of their fuel-grade ethanol to ensure it can be used for hand sanitiser.

COVID-19 is now a truly global event and is constantly evolving. So far, our global operations are coping and our people are safe. Our priority is the health and wellbeing of our people, their families and our communities. We've stopped all travel and face-to-face meetings, and are using technology to connect with each other. Take care of one another – Tātou, tātou.

“I used to think depression was this huge thing that I couldn’t deal with but then I realised that it’s about taking small steps, rather than trying to tackle the whole thing. Then we came up with the YOLO project. Each day I would take time out to do one thing that made me glad to be alive. Every day I posted my YOLO to social media, I needed a way to stay accountable. During the worst times people used to tell me to appreciate all the good things I had in life, that just made me feel even worse because I knew I had all these good things but I couldn’t enjoy them. I had to figure out what really was important to me and I realised that it was the joy of giving. Giving my time and energy to friends and family. I clearly remember at the beginning of YOLO I was like ‘oh I’m going to climb mountains, go bungy jumping’, all those sort of big statement things, but I quickly realised that’s not me, I’m not a mountain climbing type of guy. What really gives me joy is being with my family and friends, connecting and sharing with people in the community. So, while we did go skydiving for YOLO day 400 my favourite YOLO to date was actually day six when we had a bonfire on the beach and cooked pancakes with the kids.” - Wayne Langford, Fonterra Farmer and Mental Health Awareness Advocate. #MHAWNZ

The @growingfuturefarmersnz Fonterra dairy programme is expanding. 

Following positive feedback and interest from farmers and students, expressions of interest are now open for a second intake in 2027. 

The programme kicked off earlier this year with seven farmers and seven students across Waikato and Bay of Plenty, combining on-farm training with formal NZQA learning to give young people a supported pathway into dairy. 

For Fonterra farmer Annalyse Huxford, the impact is already clear. 

"It's been incredibly rewarding to see students develop new skills and grow in confidence on farm. This programme has given us hope that we can attract more young farmers and keep them engaged in the industry." 

Fonterra farmers in Waikato and Bay of Plenty can register their interest now, and young people aged 16 to 20 can apply via the Growing Future Farmers website.

It’s been one year since the launch of our Climate Roadmap, and we’re making progress towards our climate goals, including being coal free in our North Island manufacturing. 

We turned off the coal boiler at our Waitoa site this month, our last in the North Island marking a significant milestone in achieving our emissions reduction targets.
 
Here’s some key takeaway points on our progress so far:
 
🌱 Our near-term climate targets have been validated by the Science Based Targets Initiative (SBTi). This means SBTi have classified Fonterra's targets as in line with a 1.5°C future.
🌱 We’ve reduced Scope 1 and Scope 2 GHG emissions by 18.5% between FY18 and FY24.
🌱 We launched the NZMP Carbon Footprinter. This tool enables customers to understand the average emissions footprint of our key New Zealand-sourced NZMP products. 
🌱 We’ve continued to fund AgriZeroNZ, a joint venture, who have committed over $34 million in several methane mitigation technologies and R&D.
🌱 By the end of 2024 we will have achieved a 40% reduction in the number of New Zealand sites using coal from a FY18 base year.
 
Whilst we’re on track with our action plan to deliver our 2030 climate targets, there’s still more work to do.
 
Follow the link in bio to learn more about our Climate Roadmap and next steps.

Last week, our Digital team joined Mauku School and @treesforsurvivalnz to plant almost 900 trees alongside a waterway on a farm in South Auckland 🌱

Planting native trees along waterways prevents erosion, slows flooding and improves the water quality of streams and wetlands, while providing habitat for our taonga birds and insects.

Some of the trees planted included hebe, toetoe, karamū, kānuka, tī kōuka (cabbage tree) and harakeke (flax).
 
“An absolutely fantastic day planting with Mauku School and their team of supporters. The hope is that they will take away small pieces of knowledge and inspiration for the environment, all the while restoring the biodiversity to land and improving the waterways.” – Paula Marx, South Auckland Facilitator at Trees for Survival. 
 
Trees for Survival is a charitable trust which works with over 200 schools and local communities across NZ to grow and plant native trees along waterways and on erosion prone hillsides. They’re an environmental education programme teaching the importance of native plants on native ecology.

The theme for Mental Health Awareness Week this year is Five Ways, Five Days which explores a set of proven tools to boost mental health when we need it. 

Today (Wednesday) highlights being active.

Getting active in nature is a proven method of improving mental health. That’s how Surfing for Farmers (SFF) was started – to give farmers an outlet away from the pressures of work. 

The initiative runs for approximately 13 weeks from November, on a weekday evening at regional surf beaches. Surfing gear (wetsuits and surfboards) and lessons are provided free of charge. The surfing session is followed by a free BBQ where participants can get together for a yarn with fellow farmers and families. 

Over the past five years, SFF has experienced remarkable growth, expanding to 27 locations nationwide. Local coordinators generously volunteer their time to provide this invaluable opportunity, offering a respite from the all-encompassing demands of rural life and fostering social connections within the community.

Our Whānau - Te Reo Te Rangi ‘T’ - Tanker Driver, Waikato
"Pretty much my whole life’s been spent on the road. I’m always coming, going, or on the way. So it’s no surprise that I’ve had a long career in the transport industry. Yip, that sounds about right to me.
When I was growing up, life was tough. I probably experienced things some kids would not want to experience growing up. I decided I wanted to break that cycle, so at 17 I joined the NZ Army. I didn’t expect it, but it had kids from the same situation as myself, and so they became my family for more than 12 years whilst I was there. They are still my “Brothers and Sisters” from another Mother.
When I left, I knew that working in transport was another make or break moment to do something good with my life. But those long shifts on the road aren’t easy on you or the family and my early jobs took a pretty big toll, especially on the kids. I wish that could have been a bit different.
Driving for a living, there’s a lot of time to reflect. It made me want to tap into my roots and give back, and for me those roots were the Army. I’ve been a volunteer with the Order of St John for 17 years, including the last 7 years, with the New Zealand Cadet Forces. As a New Zealand Cadet Force Officer, we see kids come and go that remind me of myself. The Cadets are full of kids just like I was. We teach them how to be safe, how to be New Zealand’s next leaders. It’s life changing for them, just like it was for me.
These days, you won’t actually find me too far from home. Driving for Fonterra means I don’t have to travel those long distances. I can finally sit still and watch my kids grow up. I sometimes go down to their school and have lunch with them - we all think that’s pretty cool. Some of the other kids get envious. My kids come with me to the St John’s events and volunteer their time too, showing big and little kids alike around the ambulance. It’s nice to be able to share those lessons, make other people feel good, show respect for the jobs and roles we play in the community. All set for Mid-Winter #Christmas? Any excuse to make a #pav...⠀
A #Kiwi classic so great the #aussies tried to steal it. ⠀
RECIPE:⠀
Ingredients:⠀
6 egg whites⠀
2 cups caster Sugar⠀
1 tsp vanilla essence⠀
1 tsp white vinegar⠀
2 tsp cornflour⠀
300ml cream, whipped⠀
Berry compote⠀
Strawberries⠀
Method:⠀
Pre-heat oven to 110ºC bake (not fan bake).⠀
Line a baking tray with baking paper.⠀
In a large metal, ceramic or glass bowl (not plastic), beat the egg whites until soft peaks form.⠀
Continue beating while adding the sugar a quarter of a cup at a time. The mixture should get glossier and thicker with each addition and this should take at least 10 minutes. Beat in the vanilla, vinegar and cornflour.⠀
Spoon mixture out onto the prepared tray into a dinner plate sized mound.⠀
Bake for approximately 1 1/2 hours, until dry and crisp and it lifts easily off the baking paper. Turn the oven off and leave the pavlova for at least an hour before removing from the oven. Finish cooling on a wire rack. ⠀
When completely cool, place on a serving plate and swirl the top with the whipped cream.
To serve spoon Berry Compote over the pav and, if you have some, top with strawberries.⠀

Why not roll into your long weekend with a #Kiwifavourite? #Southland cheese roll ups are a simple and #cheesy winter warmer - and as the nights get colder, the deep south #delicacy becomes more and more enticing.
RECIPE:
Ingredients:
1 small onion - finely diced
2 garlic cloves - peeled and minced
200ml evaporated milk
½ sachet onion soup powder
250g tasty cheddar - grated
White sandwich bread
Butter - melted
Method:
In a pot, soften the onion and garlic in a dash of oil.
Once softened, add the evaporated milk, onion soup powder and grated cheese.
Stir until the cheese has melted, then continue to mix over the heat until the mixture thickens. Set aside to cool slightly.
On a slice of Tip Top bread, spread a generous layer (not too thick) of the cheese mixture over. Use your hands to make into a roll, then set onto a lined tray.
Brush with melted butter, then bake in a 180°C oven for 5 to 10 minutes or until just golden brown. Serve hot!

Issuing our first Sustainability Report is a significant milestone for us - another step forward in increasing our transparency. We know that people are not just interested in our economic performance but also our environmental performance and social performance. For many years, we've been covering that in our Annual Report. But by issuing a comprehensive Sustainability Report aligned with a recognised standard - GRI, the Global Reporting Initiative, having that externally assured, we can now satisfy that need for information in an efficient and credible way. For the first time we're covering in the report, our strategy - how that is linked with our business strategy and how it's aligned with United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, the specific ones where we can make the biggest difference through our business activities. We're also looking at all material topics - how we manage them, the commitments that we're making, the targets that we've set and the performance against those targets - the good and the challenges that we face.

If I can just give you some highlights from a people perspective. First is diversity we've got a really diverse workforce around the world and we've been bringing them together in a program called Disrupt, which helps us to foster innovation and look at solutions from a number of perspectives to really drive our business forward. We were awarded this year, the Diversity and Inclusion Award in the Deloitte Top 200 Awards, which we're really quite proud of. Interestingly, if we look at aggregate across all of our top five countries of operation, we find that women are paid on average more than men and the reason for that is that the bulk of our men are actually in probably the lower paid roles in our workforce, whereas the majority of our woman are actually in the higher paid more professional roles. And then finally a couple of last points, Health and Safety is really really important to us, really close to our heart - we want all of our people to go home safe everyday and all of the metrics that we measure, they are trending in the right direction for us, they are all reducing risk to our people and we will continue to keep a focus on reducing risk to our people. From an employee engagement perspective, we measure how engaged our employees are and how positive they feel about the company and this year, we've got the highest ratings that we've had in the seven years that we've been measuring this. So there's still some things for us to focus on from a people perspective but there's a lot of things for us to celebrate this year as well.

I want to highlight some of the key points from the climate and energy section of our new Sustainability Report. Climate change is already having an impact on agriculture globally and we know that we need to do our part to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. In our new Sustainability Report, you can find what our emissions footprint is around the world and we've found that 90% of our emissions are on farm, 9% in manufacturing and 1% are distribution. To address these emissions we have released new climate target: for operations and distribution, we're committed to net zero emissions by 2050 on the way to 100% renewable emissions. We also have an intermediate target of 30% reduction in emissions, for operation emissions from a 2015 baseline. On farm emissions are harder to address because there's no silver bullets and our farmers are already some of the lowest emission producers of dairy in the world. But we've committed to climate neutral growth for on farm emissions to 2030, which means any growth in emissions above 2015 we will voluntarily offset but we're working with our farmers on what they can do to reduce our emissions on farm. To help us achieve these new targets, we have also developed partnerships with DairyNZ on the Climate Action for Climate Change Partnership - where we are setting a framework for how farmers can contribute to the Paris Agreement and then we've partnered with the Ministry for the Environment on a road map to low emissions energy and we have an aspiration that we are going to have a positive impact on dairy emissions through enabling more innovation and sharing our knowledge. We know that climate changes are significant challenge for our industry but we're up for the challenge and we're keen to work with others on this.

Innovation starts with staying close to customers and creating alongside them. 

This week, we opened our upgraded Chengdu Application Centre in China, bringing New Zealand dairy expertise closer to customers in one of the country’s fastest-growing regions. 

Now located in a more central space in Chengdu’s Jinjiang District, the centre better empowers our technical experts, chefs and customers to develop, test and showcase food and beverage products, including applications such as cakes and beverages. 

Chengdu’s strong food culture and growing consumer market make it a natural place for Fonterra to expand its local investment. As part of our network of six application centres across China, the upgraded site will help us work closely with customers to understand changing food trends, support innovation and grow demand for New Zealand milk. 

A big thank you to everyone who helped bring this project to life. We’re excited to keep working alongside our customers to turn local insight into products Chinese consumers love, while creating more value for our farmer shareholders.

Celebrating 50 years of Pahiatua 🎉
 
This week, our team at Fonterra Pahiatua site came together to celebrate 50 years of manufacturing.
 
For half a century, the site has played an important role in the Co-op's manufacturing network, producing world-class dairy products, and contributing to the local community. Behind every milestone are the generations of people whose knowledge and commitment and have helped make Pahiatua what it is today.

A special piece of local history is getting a new lease on life 🌱 

Last week our Te Rapa whānau joined mana whenua, including Ngāti Wairere, and community partners to begin replanting the site's historic Mangaharakeke Pā.

The pā features a number of pouwhenua representing the different mana whenua groups connected to the land. 

Over time, trees had grown up around the pou, obscuring important sightlines and beginning to damage some of the carvings. Working closely with mana whenua, our Te Rapa team helped remove the problematic trees and restore views across the landscape. 

Te Rapa Environmental Advisor Te Huataki ‘Tuck’ Bradley and Environmental Manager Petra Feickert helped coordinate the planting programme, which brought together Fonterra kaimahi (employees), mana whenua and community groups to return native planting to the area.

As the new plantings take root and the pouwhenua once again stand clearly visible in the landscape, Mangaharakeke Pā will continue to tell its story, connecting people, culture and the environment. 

Petra Feickert

Matariki celebrated through Hautapu ki Hautapu, a sacred ceremony to honour the stars.​
​
Whānau from across the Co-op gathered at our Hautapu site in Waikato for a special Hautapu ki Hautapu ceremony that brought together culture, community and connection to the environment as part of this year’s Matariki celebrations. ​
​
The Hautapu ki Hautapu ceremony event began with a Matariki wānanga (education session) and included the unveiling of a new pouwhenua (pou), Wai Mate, Wai Ora.​
​
The pou symbolises the journey of water through the site’s manufacturing processes and into the new wastewater treatment plant, Wai Mahea, before treated water is respectfully returned to the whenua and the Waikato Awa.​
​
The ceremony provided an opportunity to reflect on the connections between people, water and place, while acknowledging the partnership between Fonterra and mana whenua groups Ngāti Korokī Kahukura and Ngāti Hauā. The occasion also highlighted the importance of kaitiakitanga and our collective responsibility to care for resources for future generations.​
​
“This pou tells a story of transformation and renewal. Wai Mate, Wai Ora reflects the journey of water, but it also reflects the journey of people coming together with a shared purpose and respect for the whenua.” - Pouwhenua artist Brodie Taylor.​
​
The unveiling and ceremony created a meaningful moment for everyone involved, bringing the spirit of Matariki to life through reflection, learning and connection.​
​

We’re proud that our New Zealand milk meets the requirements of the New Zealand Dairy Grass-Fed Administrative Standard, which will help to strengthen our competitive advantage in key markets across the globe.  

This standard requires that dairy animals have a diet comprised of at least 90% (fresh weight) on a 3-year rolling average of qualifying grass-fed feed types and are on pasture or forage crops for at least 8 hours per day, on average 340 days per year. 

Fonterra data shows farmers’ cows are on average 96% grass-fed and spend over 350 days on pasture*, which is above the New Zealand Grass Fed Standard’s requirements. 
 
Meeting the New Zealand Grass Fed Standard will help the Co-op strengthen relationships with customers and consumers in markets who value our grass-fed claim. At the same time, it is a point of difference in markets where suppliers cannot make such claims due to the nature of their farming systems. 
 
We appreciate the New Zealand Government and Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI) working collaboratively with the sector in the development of the standard to meet this market demand. 
 
*Our Fonterra New Zealand cows spend on average 350 days grazing on pasture and have a diet which is 96% grass, calculated on an ‘as consumed’ basis and averaged over the previous three seasons data. Grass-fed means cows mainly grazing on grass and crops in paddocks where they roam.

We start today with Mdm. Rahayu Said, Ingredient Sales Operation Executive with Fonterra, which has been part of the Singapore-New Zealand story since 16 April 1974.

We were thrilled to have a quick chat with Mdm. Rahayu.

➡️ How long have you been with the company in Singapore?
40 years. I joined on 30 October 1984 as a general clerk at the New Zealand Dairy Board, based at Quality Road in Jurong. Back then, we had a small production facility where we repacked New Zealand milk powder for export. There was a real kampung spirit, everyone helped one another, and no one stood on ceremony.

➡️ What inspired you to join the company?
It started with a job interview arranged through an employment agency. I didn’t know much about New Zealand at the time, but I knew the company had a strong reputation - especially the Anchor and NZMP brands.
What’s kept me here is the culture. Through Fonterra, I came to know the Kiwi way ; practical, down-to-earth, and very human. You feel it in the way people treat each other, how ideas are shared, and how the work gets done.

➡️ Can you share a memorable moment or achievement from your time with the company?
One of my proudest moments was hearing a top customer say, “Rahayu knows our business better than our own staff.” That really touched me. I’ve worked with some of the same customers for decades - you build trust over time. Even today, seeing our products on shelves makes me proud. It’s a nice feeling to know you had a part in getting them there.

➡️ How has your role evolved over the years and/or what new skills have you acquired?
Through the years, I’ve worn many hats - export coordinator, account assistant, and now Sales Operations Executive. But titles didn’t matter. I’ve gone from telex machines and typewriters to laptops, Power BI, and digital dashboards. Fonterra has kept up with the times and I’ve done my best to keep up too. You don’t survive 40 years without becoming a pretty good problem solver.

➡️ What about the company culture has influenced your decision to continue working at the company?
It’s the people - the heart of the company stayed the same.
Fonterra has always supported balance; between work and home, between getting things done and looking after yourself. Whether you’re working with someone from Singapore or New Zealand, you feel that shared understanding: do what’s right, be fair, and take care of one another.
There’s a Māori saying we hear a lot: “He tāngata, he tāngata, he tāngata” : it is the people, it is the people, it is the people. That’s what’s kept me here. It reminds me that we’re all different, but we belong here together.

Last week, my husband Ian and I hosted a DairyNZ event at our Te Hoe farm that showcased how we make use of technology to improve productivity on farm.

We kicked off the day by looking at how we now use AI for pasture monitoring using the Pasture.io platform. The technology means that Ian doesn't have to do long treks around the farm and instead he gets AI-driven insights every day. And using Resolution enables Ian to record critical information, data and reporting and allocate various tasks to staff. 

Senztag's national manager Jared Bekhuis talked about the wearables we use on the herd which measure rumination and ensure successful transition for their herd leading to better 6 week in calf rates and more days in milk. On our farm they have significantly reduced their empty rate after two seasons of cow manager on farm. 

But there is no one-size-fits-all when it comes to on-farm tech. We spent considerable time researching what would work for our farm - and understanding how to prioritise profitability while minimising our environmental footprint. A great example of that? We now have a lower stocking rate to reduce reliance on imported feed. While we previously milked 530 cows, Farmax Ltd modelling suggests 440 cows is our optimum.

Agritech is constantly evolving. Ian and I find it fascinating to see the advances in tools that further enhance productivity through real-time data, at the same time as giving us the ability to make decisions that also consider the environment as well as the bottom line.

Speaking of the environment, we also showed the group our stream restoration project that we've been working on since 2022 and has seen 2 hectares of riparian land planted out in natives.

Thank you to everyone who came along; there were some great questions and conversations!

Today, I joined industry colleagues in Auckland at the CDAO New Zealand conference and shared some of Fonterra’s journey in Data & AI.

Here are the key points our teams at the Co-op are working on that I covered:

- Fonterra has a rich history of #innovation, including the world’s first Whey Protein Concentrate and Spreadable Butter. Our Data & AI capabilities are built on this strong culture of innovation and collaboration.
- Our Data & AI solutions are designed to address the evolving needs and aspirations of the global markets we serve. 
- Our operations generate large volumes of data every minute, providing the exact fuel we need for leveraging #AI technologies.
- A business-led governance framework drives effective prioritization, data ownership and data quality needs.
- Our strategy and roadmap articulate how investments in Data & AI enable the delivery of our strategic choices and long-term aspirations. This is done through a Centre of Enablement working collaborative with Centre of Excellences in the business units or functions.
- We continue to invest in a #Culture of managing data as an enterprise asset and ensuring safety and responsible adoption AI. 
- We have designed and adopted an agreed Data & AI Architecture, where all partners focus on building capabilities once and using them multiple times across the business. At the Co-op every drop counts!
- Perhaps the most powerful concept we adopted is “Data Products”. These are articulated in business language and built with a clear purpose. Data Products are accessible through an Amazon-like shopping experience in a Marketplace.
- #GenAI is not a solution for all problems or opportunities.
- We are developing a #GenerativeAI platform that can leverage structured and unstructured data to support the entire workforce. This also includes a phased and sensible adoption of off-the-shelf solutions from our strategic partners: Microsoft, Databricks, Salesforce, ServiceNow, SAP, Rockwell Automation, Schneider Electric, EY and HCLTech.
- We are building the capability to deliver agents that can process “Text to Action” and execute tasks, not just chat.
- Fonterra has built an agile architecture that allows the workforce to safely and responsibly leverage the current strengths and pace of change of GenAI models.
- I believe this is the most exciting time to be a Data or AI professional!
